teile.einleitung: Dark energy is a mysterious form of energy that drives the universe apart faster and faster. So far nobody knows exactly what it is. Even so, according to current knowledge it makes up about 68 per cent of the total energy content of the universe.
wichtigste: Dark energy causes the universe to expand faster and faster.
It makes up about 68 per cent of the energy density of the universe.
The accelerating expansion was discovered in 1998 through observations of distant supernovae.
Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.
The simplest explanation is Einstein's cosmological constant of 1917.
The ESA space telescope Euclid has been studying dark energy since 2023.
What dark energy really is remains one of the greatest puzzles in physics.

abschnitte.text: Since Edwin Hubble, we have known that the universe is expanding. For a long time people believed that gravity must slow this **expansion** down. But the measurements show the opposite: the expansion is getting faster. The unknown cause of this is called **dark energy**, because it can be neither seen nor measured directly.

Two research teams observed distant exploding stars, so-called **type Ia supernovae**. These always shine with about the same brightness and are therefore suited as cosmic measuring sticks. The supernovae were fainter than expected, so further away than they should have been in a universe that is slowing down. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for this.

In 1917, Albert Einstein introduced the **cosmological constant** Λ (lambda) into his field equations. He wanted to use it to describe an unchanging universe, but later rejected the idea. Today it is the simplest explanation for dark energy: an energy that is contained in empty space itself. For it, the equation-of-state parameter w, that is, pressure divided by energy density, has the value minus 1.

Physicists have tried to calculate the energy of empty space, the **vacuum energy**, from quantum physics. The result is greater than the measured value by an unimaginable number of powers of ten. This huge discrepancy is called the **vacuum catastrophe**. Other theories suspect that dark energy changes over time, and more recent measurements give first hints of this.

The expansion has been accelerating for about 5 to 6 billion years; before that, the gravity of matter slowed it down. The ESA space telescope **Euclid** launched in 2023 and is mapping billions of galaxies in order to study dark energy and dark matter. Swiss universities such as the University of Geneva and ETH Zurich also work on Euclid. Together with dark matter, they make up about 95 per cent of the universe; only about 5 per cent is ordinary matter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stretching out of the universe.
The enormous explosion of a star, which shines very brightly.
A number in Einstein's equations that describes an energy of empty space.
Energy that is supposed to be present even in completely empty space.

gewusst: Einstein is said to have later called the cosmological constant his greatest blunder; today it is very much back in the spotlight.
The more the universe expands, the more dark energy there is in total, because every new bit of space brings it along.
Everything we can see, that is, stars, planets and gas, makes up only about 5 per cent of the universe.

teile.einleitung: A brown dwarf is an object between a planet and a star. It is too heavy to be a planet, but too light to fuse hydrogen for good like a true star.
wichtigste: Brown dwarfs lie in mass between large planets and small stars.
From about 75 Jupiter masses, an object starts burning hydrogen permanently and becomes a star.
Above about 13 Jupiter masses, brown dwarfs can fuse deuterium for a while.
They are hardly bigger than Jupiter and keep cooling down.
The term was coined by Jill Tarter in 1975.
The nearest known brown dwarfs form the Luhman 16 system.

abschnitte.text: A star shines because **hydrogen** fuses into helium in its core. This needs great heat and a lot of pressure. Below about 0.075 solar masses, which is roughly **75 to 80 Jupiter masses**, the core never gets hot enough. Such objects are called **brown dwarfs**. From about 13 Jupiter masses, however, they can fuse **deuterium** for a while. This is a heavy form of hydrogen that fuses at lower temperatures. But the supply is small and is soon used up.

Brown dwarfs have no lasting source of energy. They give off the heat that was released when they formed and **steadily cool down**. That is why they shine only faintly, mainly in infrared light. Although they can have up to about 80 times the mass of Jupiter, they are hardly bigger than it. The reason is the **degeneracy pressure** of the electrons: the particles cannot be squeezed together as tightly as you like.

The astronomer **Shiv Kumar** predicted such objects as early as 1962. The name “brown dwarf” was suggested by **Jill Tarter** in her doctoral thesis in 1975. For a long time none could be found. In 1995 **Gliese 229B** was detected as a companion of a red dwarf. Its light clearly showed **methane**, a gas that survives only at low temperatures. This made it clear that the object is much cooler than any star.

Young brown dwarfs look similar to small red dwarf stars. One clue is the element **lithium**. True stars destroy lithium quickly in their hot interiors. Brown dwarfs with a low mass never get hot enough for that, so lithium can still be found in their light. This check is called the **lithium test**.

The nearest known brown dwarfs form the **Luhman 16** system. It is a pair of two brown dwarfs that orbit each other. It lies about **6.5 light years** away. It was discovered in 2013 with data from the infrared satellite **WISE**. Because brown dwarfs shine so faintly, researchers suspect that there are still many undiscovered ones.

gewusst: To our eyes, a brown dwarf does not shine brown but rather dark red.
The coolest known brown dwarfs are colder than boiling water.

teile.einleitung: ClearSpace is a Swiss company from Lausanne that wants to collect space debris. Its satellite ClearSpace-1 is meant to remove a defunct object from orbit on behalf of ESA.
wichtigste: ClearSpace was founded in 2018 as a spin-off of EPFL in Lausanne.
The company wants to remove space debris from orbit.
In 2020, ESA ordered the mission ClearSpace-1.
The satellite is meant to catch an object with four grabbing arms.
Afterwards, both are meant to burn up in the atmosphere.
Since 2024, the old ESA satellite PROBA-1 has been the target.

abschnitte.text: Many defunct satellites, rocket parts and fragments orbit Earth. They are called **space debris**. They are very fast and can damage working satellites. If two pieces collide, even more fragments are created. That is why experts are looking for ways to clean up the orbits.

**ClearSpace** was founded in **2018** as a **spin-off** of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (**EPFL**). A spin-off is a company that grows out of a university. Its aim: to build satellites that catch defunct objects in space and dispose of them. In **2020**, the European Space Agency **ESA** ordered the mission **ClearSpace-1** for about 86 million euros. It is meant to be the first mission of its kind.

ClearSpace-1 has **four grabbing arms** that work like a claw. The satellite approaches the piece of debris, wraps around it and holds it tight. At the end it steers the pair into the **atmosphere**, where **both burn up**. This is difficult, because a dead satellite does not help: it **sends no signal** and may be **tumbling**. The catcher therefore has to navigate very precisely using cameras and sensors.

The first target was a rocket adapter called **Vespa**. In 2023, however, it was probably hit by other fragments and broke into several pieces. So in **2024**, ClearSpace-1 was given a new target: **PROBA-1**, a small ESA satellite that was launched in **2001**. The incident with Vespa shows how big the problem of space debris already is.

gewusst: Space debris often flies at several kilometres per second, faster than a bullet.
Even small fragments can punch holes in satellites.

teile.einleitung: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. It was discovered as a planet, then counted as an asteroid, and since 2006 it has been classed as a dwarf planet.
wichtigste: Ceres has a diameter of about 940 km.
It contains about 25 to 40 per cent of the mass of the whole asteroid belt.
Giuseppe Piazzi discovered it in Palermo on New Year's night 1801.
One turn on its own axis takes only about 9 hours.
Ahuna Mons is an ice volcano, and the bright spots in the crater Occator are salt.
It is named after the Roman goddess of agriculture.

abschnitte.text: The Italian priest and astronomer **Giuseppe Piazzi** observed Ceres on New Year's night 1801 at the **Palermo Observatory**. At first he took it for a comet. Then it was counted as a new **planet**. When more and more similar bodies were found between Mars and Jupiter, Ceres was long regarded as an **asteroid**. Since 2006 it has counted as one of the **dwarf planets**, like Pluto.

Ceres measures about **940 km** across. For comparison: Earth is about 12,700 km across, and Switzerland is about 350 km wide from west to east. Ceres is by far the **most massive body** between Mars and Jupiter. Depending on the estimate, it makes up about **25 to 40 per cent** of the mass of the whole asteroid belt. It is heavy enough that its own gravity has made it almost **perfectly round**.

Ceres turns once on its own axis in about **9 hours**. A day on Ceres is therefore much shorter than a day on Earth. For one trip around the Sun, however, it needs several years, because it is much further from the Sun than Earth is.

The NASA probe **Dawn** studied Ceres up close from 2015. It discovered **Ahuna Mons**, a single mountain about 4 km high. It is an **ice volcano**: it probably formed when salty ice and mud rose up from the interior. In the crater **Occator**, bright spots shine. They consist mainly of **salts** such as sodium carbonate. These probably come from salty water from the interior that evaporated at the surface.

In Roman myth, Ceres was the **goddess of agriculture** and grain. The English word **“cereal”** for breakfast flakes comes from her name. The chemical element **cerium** was also named after the object shortly after its discovery.

gewusst: Ceres was the first body in the asteroid belt ever to be discovered.
Dawn was the first space probe to orbit two different bodies one after the other: first the asteroid Vesta, then Ceres.

teile.einleitung: On 28 January 1986, the American space shuttle Challenger broke apart shortly after launch. All seven people on board were killed. The accident changed space travel and its safety rules.
wichtigste: Challenger broke apart on 28 January 1986, about 73 seconds after launch in Florida.
There were seven crew members on board, and nobody survived.
On board was the teacher Christa McAuliffe.
The cause was a sealing ring on one of the solid rocket boosters at the side.
The great cold on the day of the launch made the rubber seals hard.
It was not until September 1988 that a space shuttle flew into space again.

abschnitte.text: On **28 January 1986**, the space shuttle **Challenger** launched in Florida. About **73 seconds** after lift-off it broke apart in the air. On board were **seven crew members**, and none of them survived. Because many schools were following the launch live, millions of people saw the accident on television. It was one of the worst setbacks in the history of space travel.

On board was **Christa McAuliffe**, a teacher from the USA. She had been chosen for the **“Teacher in Space”** programme. From space she wanted to teach lessons to school classes and show children how space travel works. That is why especially many children were watching that day.

The space shuttle had two **solid rocket boosters** at its sides. Their sections were joined with rubber seals called **O-rings**. On one of the boosters, such a ring no longer sealed properly. Hot gases escaped and damaged the large **external tank** holding the fuel. This caused the shuttle to break apart. The weather played an important part: the night before the launch it was **unusually cold** in Florida, and the rubber seals became hard.

A commission investigated the accident. One of its members was the famous physicist **Richard Feynman**. He showed the cause with a simple experiment: he put a piece of sealing rubber into a glass of **ice water**. Afterwards it lost its elasticity and no longer sprang back. That way everyone could see why the seal had failed in the cold. The commission also criticised the fact that warnings from engineers had not been taken seriously enough.

After the accident, no American space shuttle flew into space for about **two and a half years**. During this time the solid rocket boosters were redesigned and the safety procedures were improved. It was not until **September 1988** that a space shuttle, **Discovery**, launched again. The accident showed how important it is to speak openly about safety concerns.

gewusst: Many schools, streets and even craters on the Moon now carry the names of the Challenger crew.
Before the accident, Challenger had already been into space successfully nine times.

teile.einleitung: Many stars do not travel alone, but have one or more companions. Two stars that are joined by gravity and orbit each other are called a binary star.
wichtigste: In a true binary star, two stars orbit a common centre of mass.
An optical double star only happens to lie in almost the same direction.
Mizar and Alcor in the Plough were regarded as an eyesight test.
Albireo in Cygnus shows an orange and a blue star in a telescope.
Algol regularly becomes dimmer because a companion passes in front of it.
Some binary stars give themselves away only through their light spectrum.

abschnitte.text: In a **true binary star**, two stars are joined by **gravity**. They orbit a **common centre of mass**. Besides these there are **optical double stars**: two stars that, seen from Earth, only happen to lie in almost the same direction. In reality they are far apart and have nothing to do with each other. There are also systems of three or more stars. They are called **multiple systems**, and with three stars a **triple system**.

In the **Plough**, the bright star **Mizar** stands in the middle of the handle. Right next to it shines the fainter little star **Alcor**. Anyone who can see the two separately has good eyes. That is why the pair used to be called the **eyesight test**. With a telescope it turns out that Mizar itself also consists of several stars.

A popular target for small telescopes is **Albireo** in the constellation **Cygnus** (the Swan). A golden-orange and a blue star stand close together. The colour reveals the temperature: blue stars are hotter, orange ones cooler. In summer, Cygnus is also high in the sky over Switzerland.

The star **Algol** in the constellation **Perseus** becomes dimmer for a few hours about every **3 days**. The reason: its two stars orbit each other in such a way that the darker one regularly passes in front of the brighter one. Such stars are called **eclipsing variables**. Other pairs are so close together that even the best telescope shows only one point. They give themselves away through their **light spectrum**: the lines shift regularly back and forth, because the stars move around each other.

Planets can also orbit binary stars. The space telescope **Kepler** discovered the planet **Kepler-16b** in 2011, which orbits a pair of two stars. Kepler looked for planets that pass in front of their star and briefly dim it. So a sky with two suns is not just imagination from films.

gewusst: A large share of the stars in the Milky Way belong to binary or multiple systems.
The name Algol comes from Arabic and means roughly “head of the demon”.

teile.einleitung: A bandage protects a wound from dirt and germs, stops bleeding or supports an injured part of the body. With a little practice you can put on a simple bandage yourself in first aid.
wichtigste: A clean, sterile dressing goes straight onto the wound first.
Over it you wrap a bandage of soft cloth.
A bandage should sit firmly but must not be too tight.
If the fingers turn blue or cold or tingle, the bandage is too tight.
For heavy bleeding a pressure bandage helps, and at the same time you call the emergency number 144.
With a triangular bandage you can tie up an injured arm.
Disposable gloves protect helpers and the injured from germs.

abschnitte.text: A bandage usually has two parts. Straight onto the wound you lay a **sterile dressing**, that is, a germ-free piece of cloth. Over it you wrap a **bandage** that holds everything in place. Bandages are made of soft cloth such as **gauze** or of stretchy fabric. For small wounds a plaster is often enough, which already combines both.

Before bandaging you put on **disposable gloves**. They protect against blood and germs. You wrap the bandage evenly, so that the layers overlap a little. The bandage should sit **firmly but not too tight**. If it is too loose, it slips off, and if it is too tight, it cuts off the blood. If fingers or toes turn blue or cold or tingle, you have to loosen the bandage.

If a wound bleeds heavily, for example on the leg, a **pressure bandage** helps. You lay on a dressing and wrap a few layers of bandage over it. Then you place a firm pad, such as a bandage that is still in its packaging, on the wound and keep wrapping. This way the bandage presses on the wound and slows the bleeding. At the same time someone calls the **emergency number 144**.

The **triangular bandage** is a large cloth in the shape of a triangle. With it you can make an **arm sling** and tie up an injured arm. This way the arm stays still and hurts less. You can also fold the cloth up and use it as a bandage or pad. There should be one in every first aid kit.

In Switzerland you often find a **first aid kit** in the car, at school and in gyms. It contains plasters, bandages, dressings, gloves, scissors and a triangular bandage. It is worth checking the contents now and then and replacing what has been used. Anyone who wants to get a driving licence in Switzerland has to attend an **emergency aid course**. There you also practise bandaging.

gewusst: A bandage is not only for wounds: an elastic bandage can also support a sprained joint.
In many communities in Switzerland, Samaritan associations offer courses in which you practise first aid.

teile.einleitung: Claudius Ptolemy was a scholar of antiquity who lived in Alexandria in Egypt. His picture of the universe with Earth at the centre shaped thinking in Europe and the Arab world for about 1,400 years.
wichtigste: Ptolemy lived from about 100 to 170 AD in Alexandria.
His main astronomical work is known as the “Almagest”.
The name “Almagest” comes from Arabic.
He explained the loops of the planets with small circles on large circles.
His star catalogue describes 48 constellations.
In the “Geographike” he collected the coordinates of about 8,000 places.

abschnitte.text: Claudius Ptolemy lived in the **2nd century AD**, from about 100 to 170. He worked in **Alexandria** in Egypt, one of the great centres of knowledge of antiquity. At that time Egypt belonged to the Roman Empire, but scholars mostly wrote in Greek. Ptolemy worked on astronomy, mathematics, geography and music.

His main astronomical work was actually called **“Mathematike Syntaxis”**. It became known under the name **Almagest**. The work reached Europe through **Arabic translations**. The name goes back to the Arabic “Al-Majisti”, which means roughly “the greatest”. The Almagest also contains a **star catalogue** with a good 1,000 stars in **48 constellations**. Many of them are still among the 88 official constellations today.

Ptolemy imagined that **Earth stands at the centre** and that the Sun, Moon and planets circle around it. One problem was the **looping movements** of the planets: sometimes they seem to run backwards across the sky. Ptolemy explained this with **small circles on large circles**. Each planet moved on a small circle, the **epicycle**, whose centre travelled along a large circle around Earth. This let him predict the positions of the planets surprisingly well.

In **geography**, too, Ptolemy wrote a famous work, the **“Geographike”**. In it he collected the coordinates of about **8,000 places**. With this information, maps of the then known world could be drawn. The work shaped mapmaking right into modern times.

abschnitte.titel: A world view with a long influence
abschnitte.text: The **Ptolemaic world view** was regarded as the authority for about **1,400 years**. It was only in the 16th and 17th centuries that the idea won through that Earth orbits the Sun. **Nicolaus Copernicus** and **Johannes Kepler** contributed most to this. Even though his world view was wrong, Ptolemy is regarded as one of the most important scientists of antiquity.

gewusst: Almost nothing is known about the life of Ptolemy, only his works survive.
A crater on the Moon and a crater on Mars carry his name.

teile.einleitung: Cepheids are stars that become brighter and dimmer in a fixed rhythm. Because their rhythm reveals their true luminosity, astronomers use them as measuring sticks for huge distances.
wichtigste: Cepheids pulsate: they expand and contract again at regular intervals.
The longer the period, the greater the luminosity.
Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered this relationship and published it in 1912.
Edwin Hubble used Cepheids to show that the Andromeda Nebula is a galaxy of its own.
The Pole Star is a Cepheid.
The class is named after the star Delta Cephei.

abschnitte.text: A Cepheid is a star that **expands and contracts** in a regular beat. As it does so, its brightness changes. Such stars lie in a narrow band in the **Hertzsprung-Russell diagram**, an overview of all stars by colour and luminosity. It is called the **instability strip**. Stars that cross this region begin to pulsate.

What drives the pulsation is called the **kappa mechanism**. In one layer of the star, helium is partly ionised. When this layer is squeezed together, it lets less radiation through, so it becomes more opaque. As a result, heat builds up, and the layer expands, cools and falls back again. Then everything starts over, like a valve that keeps opening and closing.

The American astronomer **Henrietta Swan Leavitt** found out at Harvard: the longer a Cepheid takes for one beat, the more **luminous** it is. She published this **period-luminosity relation** in 1912. If you measure the period, you therefore know the true luminosity. If you compare it with the brightness we see, you can calculate the **distance**. An example: if two Cepheids look equally bright, and one actually shines 100 times more strongly, then it is 10 times as far away, because brightness falls with the square of the distance.

In the 1920s, **Edwin Hubble** found Cepheids in the **Andromeda Nebula**. He worked out their distance and got a value far outside the Milky Way. This made it clear that Andromeda is a **galaxy of its own**. In 1952, **Walter Baade** realised that there are two types of Cepheids and that the measuring stick had been based on the wrong kind. After the correction, the distances to other galaxies were about **twice as large**.

The name comes from the star **Delta Cephei** in the constellation Cepheus. The young English astronomer **John Goodricke** discovered its changes in brightness with the naked eye in 1784. The **Pole Star** is also a classical Cepheid. It pulsates with a period of about 4 days, but its brightness varies only very slightly, so you cannot notice it without instruments.

gewusst: Henrietta Swan Leavitt worked as a so-called “computer” and analysed thousands of photographic plates of stars.
With the Hubble Space Telescope, Cepheids can even be found in galaxies that are tens of millions of light years away.

teile.einleitung: Cassini-Huygens was one of the biggest space missions to the planet Saturn. The Cassini probe orbited Saturn for over 13 years, and the Huygens lander touched down on Saturn's moon Titan.
wichtigste: NASA, ESA and the Italian space agency ASI ran the mission together.
Cassini launched in 1997 and reached Saturn's orbit on 1 July 2004.
With swing-by manoeuvres at Venus, Earth and Jupiter it gained speed.
Three radioisotope batteries supplied the power.
Huygens landed on Titan and sent data from the surface for about 72 minutes.
On 15 September 2017, Cassini was deliberately steered into Saturn's atmosphere.

abschnitte.text: The mission was a joint effort of three space organisations. The American **NASA** built the main probe Cassini. The European **ESA** built the lander **Huygens**. The Italian space agency **ASI** supplied, among other things, the large antenna for the radio link to Earth. The mission is named after the astronomers Giovanni Domenico Cassini and Christiaan Huygens, who studied Saturn in the 17th century.

Cassini launched in October 1997. For a direct flight to Saturn the probe would have needed huge amounts of fuel. So it flew past Venus twice, past Earth once and past Jupiter once, gaining momentum each time. This method is called a **swing-by** or **gravity assist**. On **1 July 2004**, Cassini swung into orbit around Saturn. Because sunlight there is about a hundred times weaker, three **radioisotope batteries** supplied the power: they turned the heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity.

In January 2005, **Huygens** landed on the large moon **Titan**. The probe ran on batteries and sent its data to Earth via Cassini. After about **72 minutes**, Cassini disappeared behind the horizon and no more surface data arrived. Using radar, Cassini later found **lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane** in Titan's polar regions. This makes Titan, besides Earth, the only known body with stable liquids on its surface.

The small moon **Enceladus** also came as a surprise. Cassini measured a slight wobble called **libration**. In 2015 it turned out to be too large for an ice shell that is firmly attached to the core. From this, researchers concluded that there is a **global ocean** of water under the ice crust. Enceladus is therefore seen as a place where conditions might be friendly to life.

From April 2017, the final phase began, the **Grand Finale**. Cassini flew 22 times through the narrow gap between the innermost ring and Saturn's atmosphere. In doing so, the gravity field and the mass of the rings were measured precisely. Because the fuel was running low, the probe was deliberately steered into the atmosphere on **15 September 2017**, where it burned up. That way it could never crash onto Titan or Enceladus and contaminate these moons with **germs from Earth**. This is called **planetary protection**.

gewusst: To this day, Huygens is the landing of a space probe that is the furthest from Earth.
During its mission, Cassini delivered hundreds of thousands of pictures of Saturn, its rings and moons.

teile.einleitung: Charon is the largest moon of the dwarf planet Pluto. Compared with Pluto it is so big that the two are often described as a double system.
wichtigste: Charon is about half the size of Pluto: roughly 1,210 km against roughly 2,380 km.
James Christy discovered Charon in 1978.
Pluto and Charon always show each other the same side.
Their common centre of mass lies outside Pluto.
One orbit takes about 6.4 days.
The probe New Horizons flew past Charon in July 2015.

abschnitte.text: The American astronomer **James Christy** discovered Charon in **1978**. On photographic plates, Pluto showed a small **bump** at its edge. This bump moved around regularly. Christy realised that it was a moon. Since then, four more, much smaller moons have been found around Pluto.

Charon measures about **1,210 kilometres**, Pluto about **2,380 kilometres**. So Charon is about **half the size** of Pluto. No other moon is so large compared with its main body. That is why the **common centre of mass** of the two lies not inside Pluto, but in the empty space between them. Both circle around this point, and Pluto visibly wobbles as it does so. This is why people often speak of a **double system**.

Our Moon always shows the same side to Earth. With Pluto and Charon this is true of **both**: they always show each other the same side. Charon circles Pluto in about **6.4 days**, and a day on Pluto lasts exactly as long. From one side of Pluto, Charon is therefore always seen in the same place in the sky, and from the other side never.

The NASA probe **New Horizons** flew past Pluto and Charon on **14 July 2015**. It had been travelling for about nine and a half years. It delivered the first close-up pictures of Charon. They showed large canyons and a strikingly **reddish north pole**. This colouring probably comes from **methane gas**, which Pluto keeps losing. Some of it reaches Charon and freezes at the cold pole. There, sunlight turns it into reddish-brown substances.

In Greek myth, **Charon** is the **ferryman** who carries the souls of the dead across the river Styx into the underworld. **Pluto** is the Roman name of the ruler of the underworld. That is why the name suits the companion of the dwarf planet.

gewusst: The red polar region of Charon was given the unofficial name “Mordor”, after a place in the books “The Lord of the Rings”.
Charon consists to a large extent of water ice.

teile.einleitung: The digestive system includes all the organs that take in food, break it down and bring the nutrients into the blood. It includes the digestive tract from the mouth to the anus and helper organs such as the liver and pancreas. Every organ has its own particular job in this long production line.
wichtigste: The digestive system consists of the digestive tract and the digestive glands.
Already in the mouth, saliva splits starch.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid.
In the small intestine most nutrients are taken into the blood.
The main job of the large intestine is to take water from the chyme.
Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
Enzymes break the nutrients down into small building blocks.

abschnitte.text: The **digestive tract** leads from the mouth through the throat, gullet, stomach, small intestine and large intestine to the anus. Together it is several metres long in adults. In addition there are glands that make digestive juices: salivary glands, the **liver** and the **pancreas**. The juices contain **enzymes** that break large nutrients down into small building blocks. This turns starch into sugar, proteins into amino acids and fat into fatty acids.

In the mouth the enzyme **amylase** in saliva already splits starch. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time. In the stomach glands in the stomach wall produce **hydrochloric acid**, which kills bacteria. The enzyme pepsin begins there to break down proteins. A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from the strong acid.

The **liver** is the largest inner organ and makes **bile**. The bile is collected in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine. There it helps to break fat into tiny droplets. The pancreas supplies enzymes for carbohydrates, proteins and fats. It also makes the hormone insulin, which regulates blood sugar.

In the **small intestine** the food is fully digested. Its inner wall is covered with millions of tiny bulges, the **villi**. They enlarge the surface enormously, so that most nutrients are taken into the blood here. The blood brings them first to the liver and then into the whole body. The small intestine is divided into the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.

The **large intestine** is shorter but wider than the small intestine. Its main job is to take **water** and salts from the chyme. This makes the rest firmer and forms it into faeces. In the large intestine live especially many bacteria, which break down indigestible fibres and make some vitamins. At the start of the large intestine hangs the **appendix**, which can become inflamed in appendicitis.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protein substance that speeds up chemical processes such as the breaking down of food.
Liquid from the liver that helps with the digestion of fat.
Tiny bulges in the small intestine that take up nutrients.
A strong acid in the stomach that kills germs.
An enzyme in saliva that splits starch.

gewusst: If you spread out the inner surface of the small intestine, it would be much larger than the skin surface of the body.
The lining of the stomach renews itself every few days, so that the acid does not harm it.
The brown colour of faeces comes from substances broken down from the bile.

teile.einleitung: The growth plate is a thin disc of cartilage in the long bones of children and teenagers. At it the bones grow in length until growth is finished at the end of adolescence.
wichtigste: The growth plate consists of cartilage.
In technical language it is called the epiphyseal plate.
It lies between the end of the bone and the shaft of the bone.
At the growth plates the long bones become longer.
The plates usually close between about 15 and 20 years.
With an X-ray of the hand the bone age can be determined.
Injuries to the growth plate have to be treated especially carefully.

abschnitte.text: A long bone such as the thigh bone has a long middle part, the **shaft**, and two thickened ends. Between the end at the joint and the shaft lies, in children, the **growth plate**. In technical language it is called the **epiphyseal plate**, because the end of the bone is called the epiphysis. Such plates are found near both ends of a long bone. On X-rays of children you see them as a narrow gap.

The growth plate is a disc of **cartilage**. Its **cartilage cells** keep multiplying. On the side of the shaft the new cartilage is gradually converted into **bone**. This way the bone becomes longer bit by bit. This growth is stimulated especially by the **growth hormone**, which is made in the pituitary gland.

At the end of growth the cartilage discs **turn completely to bone**. This usually happens between about **15 and 20 years**. After that the bones no longer grow in length. On the X-ray the gap has then disappeared. How far the plates have closed is shown by an **X-ray of the hand**: from it the doctor determines the **bone age** and estimates how much a child will still grow.

The growth plate is softer than the finished bone. That is why it can be injured in an accident. If it is damaged, the bone can go on growing **too short** or **crooked**. That is why such fractures in children are treated and checked especially carefully. Often a follow-up X-ray is taken months later.

gewusst: Not all growth plates close at the same time. Some turn to bone earlier, others only later.
Broken bones usually heal much faster in children than in adults.

teile.einleitung: Viruses are tiny germs that cause illness and are much smaller than bacteria. They cause many well-known illnesses, for example colds, flu, chickenpox or Covid-19.
wichtigste: Viruses are so small that you can usually see them only with an electron microscope.
A virus can multiply only in the cells of a living thing.
The common cold is usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses.
True flu is caused by the influenza virus.
Chickenpox is caused by the varicella zoster virus.
Flu viruses keep changing, which is why you can catch flu again and again.

abschnitte.text: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria. An ordinary light microscope is usually not enough to see them. You need an **electron microscope**, which magnifies much more strongly. A virus consists essentially of **genetic information** and a protective coat of protein. Viruses have no metabolism of their own and are therefore not counted as real living things.

A virus cannot multiply on its own. It gets into a **cell**, for example a cell of the lining of the nose. There it makes the cell produce many new viruses. These leave the cell and attack more cells. The body defends itself with its **immune system**, and this often causes fever, a runny nose or tiredness.

The **cold**, with a runny nose, sore throat and cough, is usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses. After about a week it is usually over. True **flu** is caused by the **influenza virus** and is often more serious. **Chickenpox** is caused by the varicella zoster virus, and typical are itchy blisters all over the body. Tooth decay, by contrast, is caused not by viruses but by bacteria in the mouth.

From the beginning of 2020 a new **coronavirus** spread all over the world. The illness that it causes is called **Covid-19**. Many countries, including Switzerland, took special protective measures at that time. These included keeping your distance, masks and, for a time, closed shops and schools. In a short time researchers developed vaccines against the illness.

Many viruses are passed on through small droplets when coughing and sneezing or through the hands. That is why thorough **handwashing** with soap helps. It is best to cough and sneeze into the crook of your arm. **Vaccinations** train the defences so that they recognise a virus more quickly. Flu viruses, however, keep changing a little, which is why the flu vaccine is adjusted every year.

gewusst: Antibiotics work against bacteria, but not against viruses.
There are also viruses that attack only bacteria. They are called bacteriophages.

teile.einleitung: Viruses are tiny germs that cause illness. They are much smaller than bacteria and become visible only under an electron microscope. They cannot multiply by themselves, only inside the cells of other living things. Viruses cause many well-known illnesses such as colds, flu and measles.
wichtigste: Viruses can multiply only in other cells, which is why they are not counted as independent living things.
They are usually much smaller than bacteria.
An ordinary cold is usually caused by viruses.
Flu, measles and chickenpox are also viral illnesses.
Antibiotics do not help against viruses, only against bacteria.
Vaccinations protect against many dangerous viral illnesses.
Washing your hands and sneezing into the crook of your arm slow down the spread.

abschnitte.text: At its core a **virus** consists of genetic information, that is DNA or RNA. It is surrounded by a coat of protein, and some viruses also have a coat of fat. Viruses have no metabolism of their own and cannot gain energy. That is why they can multiply only in other cells. For this reason they are usually not counted as independent **living things**.

Viruses are usually much smaller than bacteria, often only 20 to 300 nanometres in size. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. With an ordinary light microscope you therefore cannot see them, and only the **electron microscope** makes them visible. This first succeeded in the 1930s. There are, however, also giant viruses that are almost as big as small bacteria.

A virus attaches itself to a suitable **host cell** and slips its genetic information inside. The cell is thereby reprogrammed and now builds new viruses instead of its own building blocks. Often hundreds or thousands of new viruses arise this way. When they are released, the cell often dies. The new viruses attack more cells or other people.

The ordinary **cold** is usually set off by viruses, especially rhinoviruses. Other viral illnesses are flu, measles, mumps, chickenpox and Covid-19. Viruses also attack animals and plants, and there are even viruses that attack bacteria, the **bacteriophages**. **Antibiotics** work only against bacteria, so they do not help with flu. Against some viruses there are special medicines, which are called antiviral drugs.

The best protection is offered by **vaccinations**, which prepare the immune system for a particular germ. Thanks to vaccinations smallpox was wiped out worldwide by 1980. Many viruses are passed on through droplets when coughing and sneezing. Washing your hands regularly with soap, sneezing into the crook of your arm and airing rooms help to avoid infections. In Switzerland the Federal Office of Public Health recommends vaccinations against measles, mumps and rubella, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cell that a virus attacks in order to multiply inside it.
A very powerful microscope with which you can make viruses visible.
Prevention that prepares the immune system for a germ.
A virus that attacks bacteria.

gewusst: The word virus comes from Latin and means poison or slime.
Parts of our own DNA come from ancient viruses that built themselves into the genetic material of our ancestors a very long time ago.
There are more than a hundred different rhinoviruses, which is why you can get a cold again and again.

teile.einleitung: Wholemeal bread is baked from flour for which the whole grain of cereal has been ground. That is why it is usually brown and contains more dietary fibre than white bread.
wichtigste: For wholemeal flour the whole grain is ground, with husk and germ.
In white flour the husk and germ are missing.
Wholemeal bread contains more dietary fibre, also called roughage.
Because the dark husk is ground with it, wholemeal bread is usually brown.
In Switzerland wheat is the most important bread cereal, and spelt is also popular.
At least half of the cereal products should be wholegrain.

abschnitte.text: A grain of cereal consists of three parts. On the outside lies the **husk**, inside the pale **endosperm**, and at one end sits the small **germ**. For **wholemeal flour** the whole grain with all its parts is ground. For **white flour** only the pale inside is ground, and husk and germ are removed. Because the dark husk stays in wholemeal flour, wholemeal bread is usually **brown**.

Wholemeal bread contains a lot of **dietary fibre**, also called **roughage**. It is good for digestion and keeps you full for a long time. In the husk and in the germ there are also many **vitamins** and **minerals**. In white flour a large part of these is lost. That is why wholemeal bread counts as an especially valuable food.

In Switzerland **wheat** is the most important bread cereal. From wheat flour people bake, for example, the plaited loaf “Zopf” and the bread roll “Weggli”. **Spelt**, an old kind of wheat, is also very popular. It has been grown in Switzerland for a long time and baked into bread. Wholemeal bread is made from wheat, spelt or rye.

In the **food pyramid** wholemeal bread belongs to the group of **cereal products**, together with potatoes and pulses. These foods supply the body with a lot of energy. The **Swiss nutrition recommendations** advise eating at least **half** of the cereal products as wholegrain. A wholemeal bread for breakfast is a good start for this.

gewusst: In “Ruchbrot”, a typical Swiss bread, more parts of the husk stay in the flour than in white flour. That is why it is darker.
The germ is the part of the grain from which a new cereal plant can grow.

teile.einleitung: Vitamins are substances vital for life that the body needs in small amounts but usually cannot make itself. That is why we have to take them in with food, especially with fruit and vegetables. If a vitamin is missing for a long time, you can become ill.
wichtigste: The body needs vitamins for growth, defence and many metabolic processes.
Fruit and vegetables are healthy because they supply vitamins that the body needs.
Humans need 13 different vitamins.
A distinction is made between water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamins.
The skin can make vitamin D itself with the help of sunlight.
A lack of vitamins can cause illnesses such as scurvy.
With a varied diet you usually need no vitamin tablets.

abschnitte.text: **Vitamins** are substances that the body needs for many jobs, for example for fighting illnesses, healthy bones and good eyes. They supply no energy, but help to make use of nutrients. Humans need **13 vitamins**, which are named with letters, for example A, C, D, E and K. In addition there is a whole group of B vitamins. Even small amounts are enough, often only millionths of a gram a day.

Vitamins A, D, E and K are **fat-soluble**. The body can store them, and they are taken up better if you eat a little fat with them. That is why people like to add a little oil to carrots. Vitamin C and the B vitamins are **water-soluble**. The body usually gets rid of any surplus in the urine, so you need them regularly.

Vitamin C is found in peppers, kiwis, oranges and cabbage. Carrots contain a lot of **beta-carotene**, from which the body makes vitamin A, which is important for the eyes. Vitamin B12 is found almost only in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and milk. Vitamin K is found in green leafy vegetables such as spinach. People who live on a **vegan** diet have to add vitamin B12.

**Vitamin D** is a special case, because the skin can make it itself with the help of sunlight. It helps the body to take in calcium for strong bones. In Switzerland the sun in winter is often too weak for this. That is why vitamin D drops are recommended, above all for babies. Oily fish such as salmon also supplies vitamin D.

In the past sailors on long voyages suffered from **scurvy**: the gums bled, and wounds did not heal. The Scottish doctor **James Lind** showed in 1747 that citrus fruits help, and today we know that vitamin C was missing. The name vitamin was coined in 1912 by the biochemist **Casimir Funk**. A lack of vitamin D leads in children to rickets, with soft, bent bones. Too much of a fat-soluble vitamin from tablets can, however, also do harm.

begriffe.erklaerung: Dissolves in fat and can be stored in the body.
Dissolves in water, and any surplus is got rid of.
An illness caused by a lack of vitamin C.
The orange pigment in carrots, from which the body makes vitamin A.

gewusst: Most animals can make vitamin C themselves, but humans, apes and guinea pigs cannot.
The word vitamin is made up of the Latin vita for life and the word amine.
A pepper often contains more vitamin C than an orange of the same weight.

teile.einleitung: The Chandrasekhar limit is the greatest mass a white dwarf can have. It is about 1.4 solar masses. If a white dwarf becomes heavier, it can no longer hold itself up against its own gravity.
wichtigste: A white dwarf is the burnt-out core of a star.
It is held up by the degeneracy pressure of the electrons.
The limiting mass is about 1.4 solar masses.
Chandrasekhar calculated it in 1930 on a ship journey to England.
Arthur Eddington publicly rejected the result in 1935.
In 1983, Chandrasekhar received the Nobel Prize in Physics.

abschnitte.text: When a star like the Sun has used up its fuel, a small, very dense remnant is left: a **white dwarf**. It mostly consists of **carbon and oxygen**, because the star had earlier fused helium into these elements. It was too light for any further fusion. In the white dwarf, no more nuclear fusion takes place. It is about as big as Earth, but has roughly as much mass as the Sun.

Without fusion, the heat that puffs a star up from inside is missing. Something else holds the white dwarf up: the **degeneracy pressure of the electrons**. According to the **Pauli principle**, electrons cannot move as close together as you like. They resist being squeezed together. Strangely, the **more mass** a white dwarf has, the **smaller** it becomes, because the stronger gravity packs the electrons more tightly.

At very high density, the electrons move at almost the **speed of light**. They are said to become **relativistic**. Then their pressure no longer grows fast enough to hold back gravity. Above about **1.4 solar masses**, the white dwarf therefore collapses. The exact value depends on how many nuclear particles, that is, **nucleons**, there are per electron. For carbon and oxygen it is 2.

The young Indian student **Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar** travelled by ship from India to England in 1930 to study there. During the crossing he combined the **theory of relativity** with quantum physics and so found the upper limit for the mass of white dwarfs. In 1935 the famous astrophysicist **Arthur Eddington** sharply criticised the idea at a meeting of the Royal Astronomical Society. With time, however, Chandrasekhar's result won through.

In **1983**, Chandrasekhar received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for his work on the structure and evolution of stars. He shared the prize with **William Fowler**. Today the Chandrasekhar limit is important for understanding why some stellar remnants explode or turn into neutron stars.

gewusst: A spoonful of material from a white dwarf would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
An X-ray telescope of NASA was called “Chandra” in honour of the researcher.

teile.einleitung: Veins are blood vessels that bring the blood from the whole body back to the heart. You can even see some of them as bluish lines under the skin, for example at the wrist.
wichtigste: Veins carry the blood back to the heart.
Through the skin veins look bluish, but the blood in them is dark red.
Veins have a thinner wall than arteries, because there is little pressure in them.
In the veins of the legs, vein valves stop the blood from flowing back.
Working leg muscles press on the veins and push the blood upwards.
When blood is taken, it is usually taken from a vein in the crook of the arm.

abschnitte.titel: The way back to the heart
abschnitte.text: The heart pumps blood through the **arteries** into the whole body. In the organs the blood gives up oxygen and nutrients. After that the **veins** collect the blood again. Small veins flow together into ever larger ones. The largest veins, the **venae cavae**, finally open into the heart.

At the wrist or on the back of the hand you can see veins as **bluish** lines. The blood in them is not blue, however, but **dark red**. It has less oxygen than the bright red blood in the arteries. That the veins look blue is due to the skin: it lets red light through differently from blue. That is why you see a bluish shimmer from outside.

In the legs the blood has to flow upwards against gravity. The **vein valves** help with this. Like small doors they open in only one direction, namely towards the heart. When you walk or run, the **leg muscles** press on the veins. This pushes the blood upwards bit by bit.

In the veins the blood flows at low pressure. That is why their wall is **thinner** than the wall of the arteries. Veins, however, are stretchy and can hold a lot of blood. If you let your hand hang down, the blood flows back more slowly. The veins on the back of the hand then fill up and stand out clearly.

If a doctor needs a blood sample, she usually takes the blood from a vein in the **crook of the arm**. There the veins lie just under the skin. Beforehand a band is put around the upper arm, so that the vein fills well. Then she puts a fine needle in. In the laboratory you can measure, for example, sugar or iron in the blood.

gewusst: The largest part of the blood in the body is in the veins.
The pulmonary veins are an exception: they bring oxygen-rich, bright red blood from the lungs to the heart.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin D is important for strong bones. The body makes it mainly itself in the skin when sunlight falls on it. In the Swiss winter the sun is often not enough for this, and a deficiency can arise.
wichtigste: The skin makes vitamin D with the help of UVB radiation.
In winter the sun in Switzerland stands too low, so hardly any UVB arrives.
Vitamin D3 is called cholecalciferol.
The liver makes calcidiol from it, and the kidney makes the active calcitriol.
Vitamin D encourages the uptake of calcium in the gut.
The vitamin D status is measured through the blood value 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Infants in Switzerland receive vitamin D drops from birth.

abschnitte.text: Unlike most vitamins, the body can make vitamin D itself. For this the skin needs **UVB radiation** from sunlight. In the skin it converts 7-dehydrocholesterol into a precursor of **vitamin D3**. Vitamin D3 is chemically called **cholecalciferol** and is also often used in supplements. Besides it there is vitamin D2, ergocalciferol from mushrooms.

abschnitte.titel: Why a deficiency threatens in winter
abschnitte.text: In winter the sun in Switzerland stands **low**. Its light then has a long way through the atmosphere. The **ozone layer** filters the UVB largely out. So in the winter months the skin hardly makes any vitamin D. People who are also outdoors little have a higher risk of **vitamin D deficiency**.

Vitamin D is converted in the body in two steps. First the **liver** makes **calcidiol** from it, which is the storage form in the blood. Then the **kidney** converts it into the active hormone form **calcitriol**. Calcitriol encourages the uptake of **calcium** in the gut. It increases the production of transport proteins that bring calcium into the blood, and the body needs calcium for firm bones.

To check the supply, you measure **25-hydroxyvitamin D** in the blood, that is calcidiol. It shows the supply over the last weeks. Good natural sources are rare, and one of them is **oily fish** such as herring, salmon or mackerel. That is why you take supplements when needed. The amount is given in micrograms or in **international units**: 1 microgram corresponds to 40 IU, so 20 micrograms to 800 IU.

In Switzerland **infants** routinely receive **vitamin D drops** from birth. Babies should not be in the blazing sun, and from food they get too little vitamin D. The daily dose protects their growing bones. In a severe deficiency in children the bones can become soft and deformed. This illness is called **rickets**.

gewusst: Rickets used to be widespread in industrial cities with a lot of smoke and little sun. It was also called the “English disease”.
Cod liver oil, an oil from the liver of cod, used to be given to children by the spoonful against vitamin D deficiency.

teile.einleitung: A vibration is a quick trembling to and fro. We feel it with the skin, for example when the phone buzzes in a trouser pocket or a heavy lorry drives past.
wichtigste: A vibration is a quick oscillation, that is, a trembling to and fro.
In a phone a small motor produces the vibration.
When you hum, the vocal cords in the larynx oscillate.
A seismograph measures the shaking of earthquakes.
Deaf people can feel music through vibrations.
Spiders notice from the trembling of the web that an insect is caught.

abschnitte.text: In a **vibration** something moves very quickly to and fro. This is also called an **oscillation**. How often something oscillates per second is measured in **hertz**. In the skin there are special **touch corpuscles** that sense such fine shaking. That is why we feel vibrations even when we hear nothing.

In a phone a small **motor** turns very fast. It makes the device tremble, and you feel it on your skin. It is similar with the **electric toothbrush**: a motor moves the brush head very fast. When a heavy lorry drives close by, it even makes the **ground** oscillate. You feel this vibration with your feet.

Every note arises from an oscillation. If you pluck a **guitar string**, it swings to and fro and produces the note. With your fingers you feel a fine trembling. When you hum, the **vocal cords** in the larynx also oscillate. If you put your hand to your throat, you can feel it. Loud music makes the ground and the air oscillate, which is why **deaf** people can feel the bass with their whole body.

Many animals use vibrations to sense their surroundings. A **spider** often sits at the edge of its web. If a trapped insect struggles, it makes the threads oscillate. The spider feels this with its legs and knows at once where the prey is. Fish, too, feel fine movements in the water with their lateral line organ.

In an **earthquake** the ground shakes. A **seismograph** records even the smallest ground movements. In Switzerland the **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich measures with many stations across the whole country. Most earthquakes in Switzerland are so weak that you do not feel them. The instruments register them all the same.

gewusst: Strong vibrations from tools such as pneumatic drills can in the long run strain hands and joints. That is why there are protective rules at work.
Elephants can sense through the ground vibrations that come from other elephants far away.

teile.einleitung: Atrial fibrillation is a heart rhythm disorder in which the atria of the heart twitch chaotically instead of contracting in an orderly way. It is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder and affects mainly older people.
wichtigste: In atrial fibrillation the atria are excited in a disorderly way about 350 to 600 times a minute.
In the ECG the P waves are missing, and the intervals between the heartbeats are irregular.
The most dangerous result is a stroke caused by a blood clot.
The CHA2DS2-VASc score helps to estimate the risk of stroke.
An electrical cardioversion can restore the normal rhythm.
In catheter ablation the openings of the pulmonary veins are electrically isolated.

abschnitte.text: Normally the **sinus node** sets the rhythm of the heart. In **atrial fibrillation**, by contrast, many excitations circle through the atria in a disorderly way. They are excited about **350 to 600 times per minute**. An orderly contraction is then no longer possible, and the atria only twitch. The ventricles beat completely irregularly in the process, which is called **absolute arrhythmia**.

With an **ECG**, atrial fibrillation can be recognised well. Because the atria are not excited in an orderly way, the **P waves** are missing. The intervals between the ventricular beats, the **RR intervals**, are irregular. Many of those affected feel their heart skipping, racing or shortness of breath. Others notice nothing at all, and the fibrillation is found by chance.

In the fibrillating atria the blood flows slowly. Above all in the left **atrial appendage** it can clot. If such a **clot** comes loose, it can travel with the bloodstream to the brain and block an artery there. This leads to a **stroke**. To estimate the risk, the **CHA2DS2-VASc score** is used. It counts risk factors such as age, high blood pressure, diabetes and earlier strokes, and the higher it is, the more likely it is that blood thinning is needed.

In **electrical cardioversion**, under a short anaesthetic, an electric shock timed to the ECG is delivered. In it all the heart muscle cells are excited at the same time, and afterwards the sinus node often takes over again. Disturbing sources of excitation often sit at the **openings of the pulmonary veins**. In **pulmonary vein isolation**, a form of catheter ablation, these places are electrically cut off from the atrium by scarring. Medicines can also regulate the rhythm or the heart rate.

Atrial fibrillation is distinguished by its duration. **Paroxysmal** atrial fibrillation occurs in attacks and stops again by itself. It usually ends within 48 hours, at the latest after 7 days. If it lasts longer, it is called **persistent** atrial fibrillation. The risk of atrial fibrillation rises clearly with **age**.

gewusst: Many smartwatches can now detect an irregular pulse and so give a hint of atrial fibrillation.
The word “paroxysmal” comes from Greek and means “in attacks”.

teile.einleitung: CHEOPS is a space telescope that measures planets around other stars precisely. It is a mission of ESA in which Switzerland and the University of Bern play the leading role.
wichtigste: CHEOPS is an ESA mission, scientifically led by the University of Bern.
The telescope launched in December 2019 on a Soyuz rocket.
It studies known exoplanets and determines their size.
To do so it uses the transit method: the star briefly becomes slightly dimmer.
CHEOPS orbits at a height of about 700 km, passing over the poles.
On board are 2,748 reduced children's drawings on two titanium plates.

abschnitte.text: **CHEOPS** is a mission of the European Space Agency **ESA**. Switzerland is its most important partner. The **University of Bern** leads a consortium from eleven countries and is responsible for the science. The telescope was built in Switzerland and in other European countries. On 18 December 2019, CHEOPS launched on a **Soyuz rocket** from the European spaceport in French Guiana.

CHEOPS does not search for new planets, but measures **known exoplanets** very precisely. Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars other than the Sun. When such a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a little light, and the star becomes **slightly dimmer** for a short time. This method is called the **transit method**. The bigger the planet, the more light disappears. That is how its size can be calculated.

abschnitte.titel: A planet like a rugby ball
abschnitte.text: One well-known measurement concerns the planet **WASP-103b**. It orbits very close to its star. The star's strong **tidal forces** stretch it out lengthwise. According to the CHEOPS measurements, it is therefore not round, but shaped like a **rugby ball**. In 2023, CHEOPS also helped to detect a **ring** around the dwarf planet **Quaoar** at the edge of the Solar System, a ring that lies surprisingly far out.

CHEOPS flies around Earth at a height of about **700 km**, passing over the **poles**. The orbit is chosen so that the Sun is always at roughly the same angle to the satellite. This matters for very precise brightness measurements, because the conditions then hardly change. The telescope always looks away from the Sun, so that no sunlight disturbs it.

Children were able to submit drawings for CHEOPS. **2,748** of them were drawn by lot, greatly reduced in size and engraved on two **titanium plates**. These plates now fly with the satellite around Earth. In this way, many young people have become a small part of this space mission.

gewusst: CHEOPS stands for “CHaracterising ExOPlanet Satellite”.
Bern has a long tradition in space travel: even on the first Moon landing in 1969, the astronauts set up a solar wind sail from the University of Bern.

teile.einleitung: Vein valves are small valves in the veins. They make sure that the blood flows in only one direction, namely towards the heart. They are especially important in the legs.
wichtigste: Vein valves stop the blood in the veins from flowing back.
They are pocket-shaped folds of the innermost wall layer of the vein.
In the legs there are especially many vein valves.
Together with the leg muscles they form the muscle pump.
The large venae cavae have no valves.
If the valves close poorly, varicose veins can develop.

abschnitte.text: Vein valves are small **pockets** on the inner wall of the veins. When the blood flows towards the heart, they lie flat against the wall and let it through. If the blood wants to flow back, the pockets fill and close the vein. This way they act like **valves** that open in only one direction. They are folds of the **intima**, the innermost wall layer, and are covered with endothelium.

In the legs the blood has to flow upwards against **gravity**. That is why leg veins have especially many valves. When the leg muscles tense, they press on the deep veins. The valves make sure that the blood then flows only upwards. This mechanism is called the **muscle pump**. People who walk a lot therefore help the blood on its way to the heart.

Not all veins have valves. The upper and lower **vena cava**, which open directly into the heart, have none. There the blood is drawn in mainly by the **suction** of breathing and the heart. When you breathe in, a negative pressure arises in the chest that pulls the blood towards the heart. The heart itself also sucks in blood as it relaxes.

If the valves in the surface veins of the legs no longer close properly, the blood backs up. The veins widen and become twisted: **varicose veins** develop, medically **varices**. If the blood congestion lasts a long time, it is called **chronic venous insufficiency**. Then the legs swell, the skin changes colour and, in the worst case, an open leg ulcer develops. Compression stockings and exercise can help.

Vein valves played an important part in the history of medicine. The English doctor **William Harvey** published his teaching on the **circulation of the blood** in 1628. As an argument he used the vein valves: they let the blood flow only towards the heart. This did not fit the old idea that blood flows back and forth in the veins. So the valves helped to prove the closed circulation.

gewusst: Harvey had studied in Padua, where his teacher Hieronymus Fabricius had described the vein valves precisely.
With a simple experiment on the forearm, Harvey was able to show that blood in the veins cannot be pushed away from the heart.

teile.einleitung: A rotating star chart shows which stars and constellations you can see in the sky at a particular time. You set the date and time, and the right night sky appears in the window.
wichtigste: You set the date and the time against each other.
The edge of the oval window shows the horizon.
The star disc turns around the Pole Star.
A chart is only valid for one particular geographical latitude, for Switzerland about 47 degrees north.
In summer you have to subtract one hour because of summer time.
Planets are not drawn in, because they wander through the constellations.

abschnitte.text: A rotating star chart consists of two discs. At the bottom is the **star disc** with all the stars, and above it the **cover disc** with an oval window. The **dates** are written around the edge of the star disc, and the **times** around the edge of the cover disc. If you turn the time you want over today's date, the window shows the matching sky. The star disc turns around the **Pole Star**, which stands almost exactly at the celestial north pole. All the other stars seem to turn around it during the night.

The edge of the oval window shows the **horizon**. Only the stars inside the window are currently above the horizon and visible. Stars outside it have set at that time. Because the visible part of the sky depends on the **geographical latitude**, a chart is valid only for one particular latitude. The further north you live, the more stars stay above the horizon all the time, and the fewer southern stars you see. For Switzerland, a chart for about **47 degrees north** is suitable.

On a star chart, **east is on the left** when north is at the top. On a map it is the other way round. The reason: you look at a map from above, but at the sky from below. If you hold the star chart **above your head** and look up, the directions are right again. It is best to hold the edge with the direction you are facing downwards.

Many star charts are set to **standard time**, in Switzerland Central European Time (CET). In summer, however, **summer time** applies, which is one hour ahead. That is why in summer you have to **subtract one hour**. If the clock shows 11 pm, you set the chart to 10 pm.

At night, it is best to read the chart with **red light**. Weak red light hardly dazzles eyes that have got used to the dark. White light would spoil your **night vision** for a long time. **Planets** are not marked on the chart permanently, because they wander through the constellations over weeks and months. You look up their position in an astronomical **yearbook**.

gewusst: The eyes need about half an hour until they have got fully used to the dark.
A rotating star chart works without electricity and without the internet, year after year.

teile.einleitung: The vestibular organ is our organ of balance. It lies well protected in the inner ear and reports to the brain how we turn, tilt or accelerate the head.
wichtigste: The vestibular organ lies in the labyrinth of the inner ear, right next to the cochlea.
Each side has three semicircular canals, which detect turns in all directions.
The utricle and saccule report gravity and acceleration in a straight line.
The otoliths are tiny crystals of calcium carbonate.
The vestibulo-ocular reflex keeps your gaze steady when the head moves.
Robert Bárány received the Nobel Prize in 1914 for his research on the organ of balance.

abschnitte.titel: An organ in the inner ear
abschnitte.text: The organ of balance lies in the **labyrinth** of the inner ear, right next to the **cochlea**. Both are filled with a liquid, the **endolymph**. The vestibular organ consists of two parts: the three **semicircular canals** and two small sacs called the **utricle** and **saccule**. On each side of the head there is one such organ. Its signals run to the brain through a nerve.

Each inner ear has **three semicircular canals**, which stand roughly at right angles to each other. This way turns in all directions of space can be detected. When you turn your head, the endolymph, because of its inertia, lags behind a little. In doing so it bends fine **sensory hairs**, which inform the brain about the turn. If you spin round in a circle for a long time and then stop, the liquid flows on a little further, and you feel dizzy.

In the utricle and saccule lie the **macular organs**. They carry a membrane with tiny crystals, the **otoliths** or ear stones. These consist of **calcium carbonate** and are heavier than their surroundings. That is why the membrane shifts when you tilt your head or accelerate straight ahead. This is how you feel **gravity**, for example in a lift or when a train pulls away.

When the organ of balance reports a turn of the head, the eyes at once move just as fast in the opposite direction. This is the **vestibulo-ocular reflex**. This way the picture on the retina stays steady. If the eyes and the organ of balance report contradictory things, this can lead to **travel sickness**. If you read in a car, for example, the eyes report rest, but the organ of balance reports movement. This conflict of the senses can cause nausea and dizziness.

In the **caloric test** the doctor flushes warm and cold water into the ear canal. The change in temperature creates a flow of the endolymph in the lateral semicircular canal. The eye movements this sets off show whether the organ on each side works. A common disorder is **benign positional vertigo**. In it, loosened ear stones get into a semicircular canal and fake a turn. With targeted positioning manoeuvres they can be moved back.

gewusst: The Austrian ear doctor Robert Bárány received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1914 for his research on the vestibular apparatus.
The organ of balance also works in the dark and with your eyes closed: you still feel whether you are lying, standing or turning.

teile.einleitung: In constipation, bowel movements are rare, and the stools are hard. This is unpleasant but common. With the right diet and enough exercise you can often do a lot about it.
wichtigste: In constipation the stools are rare, hard and difficult to pass.
The technical term for it is obstipation.
Healthy is about three bowel movements a day to three a week.
Fibre and drinking enough help most.
Exercise stimulates the activity of the gut.
People who often suppress the urge weaken the signal over time.

abschnitte.text: In constipation **bowel movements** are rare, and the stools are often hard and difficult. This can cause **stomach ache** and a feeling of fullness. In technical language constipation is called **obstipation**. The word comes from the Latin “obstipare”, which means to stuff full. In adults it is usually called constipation when the bowels move less than three times a week.

**Fibre** is made up of parts of plants that the body cannot digest. It binds water and makes the stools softer and bulkier. A lot of fibre is found in **wholemeal bread**, vegetables, pulses and fruit. Animal foods such as meat or cheese contain almost none. For fibre to work well, the body also needs enough **liquid**, best of all water.

Physical **exercise** also gets the gut going. Running, cycling or swimming stimulate the activity of the gut. People who sit a lot are more likely to get constipation. It is also important to give in to the **urge to go**. People who often suppress it get the gut used to it, the signal becomes weaker, and the stools stay longer in the gut.

Medicines that encourage bowel movements are called **laxatives**. They make the stools softer or stimulate the gut. You should take them only for a short time and after medical advice. Often it is enough to change your diet. If you have severe stomach pain, blood in the stools or constipation that lasts a long time, you belong with the doctor.

gewusst: The large intestine takes water from the food pulp. The longer the stools stay there, the harder they become.
On journeys many people get constipation, because eating, drinking and the daily routine change.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin C is a nutrient vital for life that we have to take in with our food. The body needs it above all for a strong immune system and healthy connective tissue. Many people think of lemons, but red peppers and rose hips contain even more of it.
wichtigste: Chemically, vitamin C is called ascorbic acid.
The body needs it for a strong immune system and healthy connective tissue.
Humans cannot make vitamin C themselves and have to eat it.
A lot of vitamin C is found in peppers, citrus fruits, kiwis, berries and cabbage.
Vitamin C dissolves in water and is partly lost in long cooking.
A severe deficiency leads to the illness scurvy.
In 1933 the Swiss chemist Tadeus Reichstein developed a process to make vitamin C artificially.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs it for
abschnitte.text: Vitamin C helps the **defence cells** of the **immune system** to fight germs that cause illness. The body also needs it to make **collagen**. Collagen is a protein that makes skin, bones, teeth, gums and blood vessels firm and elastic. That is why wounds heal better with enough vitamin C. It also helps the gut to take up iron from plant food.

**Citrus fruits** such as oranges and lemons are well known. Even more vitamin C, however, is contained in red peppers, rose hips, sea buckthorn and blackcurrants. Kiwis, strawberries, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and potatoes also supply a lot of it. People who eat fruit and vegetables every day usually get enough.

Vitamin C is **water-soluble**, so it dissolves in the cooking water. Heat, light and air destroy it little by little. That is why raw or briefly steamed vegetables contain more vitamin C than those cooked for a long time. Freshly squeezed juice should be drunk quickly. The body gets rid of surplus vitamin C through the kidneys in the urine.

If vitamin C is missing for weeks, the illness **scurvy** develops. In it the gums bleed, teeth fall out and wounds heal badly. In the past many sailors on long sea voyages suffered from it, because they had no fresh fruit. The Scottish doctor **James Lind** showed in an experiment in 1747 that citrus fruits help against scurvy. Today scurvy is very rare in Switzerland.

The Hungarian researcher **Albert Szent-Györgyi** obtained vitamin C from peppers around 1930 and received the Nobel Prize in 1937. The Swiss chemist **Tadeus Reichstein** found a way in 1933 to make vitamin C artificially in large amounts. His process was used in industry for a long time. Today vitamin C is also added to foods so that they stay fresh longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical name of vitamin C.
A protein that makes skin, bones and blood vessels stable.
An illness that arises from a severe lack of vitamin C.
A substance that dissolves in water.

gewusst: Most animals can make vitamin C themselves, but humans, apes and guinea pigs cannot.
Red peppers contain about twice as much vitamin C as a lemon.
On food packaging vitamin C is often given as E 300.

teile.einleitung: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that is important above all for good eyesight. The body takes it in from animal foods or makes it from the orange pigment beta-carotene.
wichtigste: Chemically, vitamin A is called retinol.
Beta-carotene from carrots is a precursor of vitamin A.
Vitamin A is fat-soluble, so it is taken up better with a little fat.
A deficiency can lead to night blindness.
The liver stores vitamin A, which is why liver as a food is very rich in it.
Too much vitamin A from supplements can be harmful.
Golden Rice was developed, among other places, at ETH Zurich.

abschnitte.text: Vitamin A is chemically called **retinol**. The name recalls the **retina** of the eye. In the **rods** of the retina vitamin A is used to make **visual purple**, also called rhodopsin. It makes seeing in dim light possible. If vitamin A is missing, you see badly at dusk: this is called **night blindness**.

The orange pigment in carrots is called **beta-carotene**. It is a **precursor** of vitamin A, which the body converts when needed. Beta-carotene is also found in pumpkin, apricots and peppers. Because vitamin A and its precursor are **fat-soluble**, it is best to prepare carrots with a little oil or butter. This way the gut can take them up much better.

The **liver** builds up large reserves of vitamin A. That is why liver as a food contains a great deal of it. Eggs, butter and dairy products also supply vitamin A. What the body does not need is not simply got rid of in the urine but **stored**. If you take very large amounts through supplements, the vitamin can build up and poison you. With normal food this hardly happens.

In poor countries **vitamin A deficiency** is still common today. To help, researchers developed **Golden Rice**. This genetically modified variety of rice makes a precursor of vitamin A in the grain and is therefore yellowish. It was developed by **Ingo Potrykus** of ETH Zurich and **Peter Beyer**. The use of genetically modified plants is still debated today.

gewusst: The liver of polar bears contains so much vitamin A that even a small amount can be poisonous for humans.
If you eat a great many carrots, the skin can turn slightly orange. This is harmless and goes away again.

teile.einleitung: Scales measure how heavy something is. There are scales for people, for babies, for the kitchen and even very simple balance scales that compare two things with each other.
wichtigste: With bathroom scales you measure body weight in kilograms.
If nobody stands on the scales, they show 0 kg.
In the kitchen you weigh out ingredients with kitchen scales, usually in grams.
On balance scales the heavier side sinks down.
Babies are weighed at the paediatrician on baby scales.
If you want to compare your weight, you always weigh yourself at the same time of day.

abschnitte.text: With **bathroom scales** you measure body weight. They show how many **kilograms** you weigh. If nobody stands on them, nothing presses on the scales, and they show **zero**. A thermometer, by contrast, measures temperature, not weight. Many bathroom scales today are digital and show the weight as a number.

You can also calculate with scales. Nina weighs 25 kg, her **school bag** weighs 3 kg. If she stands on the scales with the school bag, they show 25 plus 3, so **28 kg**. You can also subtract: Mum weighs 68 kg with the baby and 62 kg without the baby. 68 minus 62 makes **6 kg**, so that is how heavy the baby is.

In the kitchen you need **kitchen scales**. With them you weigh out flour, sugar or butter for cooking and baking, usually in **grams**. At the paediatrician there are **baby scales**.
